lessons.title: Staffing an aquaculture operation
lessons.html:
People keep fish alive

An aquaculture farm runs every day of the year, often with night checks on aeration and oxygen. A missed feed, an unnoticed pump failure or careless handling by one worker can cost thousands of rand. Human resources management is about having the right people, with the right skills, on the right shift, working safely and fairly.

Planning staff needs

  • List all recurring tasks: feeding rounds, water testing, cleaning, grading, harvesting, maintenance, security and night checks.
  • Estimate hours per task per week, including peak periods such as harvest and restocking.
  • Build a roster that covers weekends, public holidays and night standby.
  • Identify critical skills (water testing, generator operation, first aid) and make sure at least two people hold each one.

Recruitment and selection

  1. Write a clear job description: duties, hours, physical requirements such as work in water, and reporting line.
  2. Advertise locally; rural farms often recruit from nearby communities.
  3. Shortlist against the job requirements, not personal connections.
  4. Interview with the same questions for each candidate and, where practical, a short practical test.
  5. Check references and confirm the right to work.
  6. Issue a written contract and induct the new worker.

Induction

Induction should cover farm layout, safety rules (water, electricity, chemicals), biosecurity, the daily routine, record-keeping, who to call in an emergency, pay and leave arrangements. Pair new staff with an experienced mentor for the first weeks.

The legal framework

Key South African laws include the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 (working hours, leave, written particulars), the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 (fair dismissal and dispute resolution), the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 (no unfair discrimination), the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 and the Skills Development Act 97 of 1998. Sectoral determinations for farm workers set minimum conditions; check current requirements with your HR adviser or the Department of Employment and Labour.

lessons.title: Developing and managing the team
lessons.html:
Training and skills

Aquaculture skills are specialised and not widely available in rural areas, so farms grow their own. Use a skills matrix: list workers down the side, tasks across the top, and mark each person as trainee, competent or able to train others. This shows gaps and who can cover for whom.

  • Combine on-the-job coaching with accredited learning such as the Aquaculture Farm Worker occupational certificate.
  • Keep training records; they support skills levy claims and show due diligence for safety.
  • Use workplace experience logbooks for learners and sign them off honestly.

Performance management

Set clear, measurable expectations: for example, all units fed on time, water readings recorded twice daily, mortalities logged daily. Review regularly in short one-on-one conversations. Recognise good work; feedback should be specific and timely.

Discipline and grievances

Have a written disciplinary code and grievance procedure that workers understand. Discipline should be consistent, aimed at correcting behaviour, and follow a fair procedure: investigate, give the worker a chance to respond, decide, and record the outcome. For serious matters seek HR or labour-law advice before acting.

Health, safety and wellbeing

  • Provide protective equipment: gumboots or waders, gloves, eye protection, rain gear.
  • Train in water safety and never allow lone working in deep ponds.
  • Appoint and train first aiders through an accredited provider.
  • Manage fatigue on night standby and long harvest days.

Communication

Hold short daily briefings at shift start: priorities, problems from the previous shift, and safety reminders. Post rosters and procedures where everyone can see them, in the languages your staff use.

Key points

  • Plan staffing to cover every day, nights and peak periods.
  • Recruit fairly against a written job description.
  • Use a skills matrix to plan training and cover.
  • Apply discipline consistently and with a fair procedure.
  • Comply with labour law and the OHS Act; seek advice on complex matters.
